A satellite imagery shows Bab al-Mandeb Strait on July 12, 2026 [File: Nasa Worldview/Handout via Reuters]
This week, there has been some cautious optimism about a de-escalation in the US-Israel war on Iran. Qatari and Pakistani mediators have intensified efforts to conclude a deal between the warring sides after a massive military build-up in the region raised fears of a renewed kinetic phase of the conflict.
There are various factors that have played into the decision of US President Donald Trump to hold off on new attacks for now. One of them is certainly Iran’s ability to see an assault coming and retaliate with precision – a capability that is likely made possible by Russian military-grade geospatial and signals intelligence.
For eight months now, Project AURORAH, which I founded, has followed the trajectories of Russian spy satellites. It has identified at least 20 Russian spacecraft in the Kosmos-2600 series, 18 of which can be tracked.
I focus on this group because it includes Russia’s newest and most manoeuvrable military reconnaissance satellites. They can provide military cartographic reconnaissance of installations and terrain, as well as optical imagery, radar observation, and signals intelligence collection, including radar and other radio frequency emissions and military communications activity.
The satellites I have followed cover an area that extends from Syria, Lebanon and Israel to Jordan, Saudi Arabia, the wider Arabian Peninsula, Iraq and Iran, including both Bab al-Mandeb and the Strait of Hormuz. Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan, one of the eight remaining candidates to be the next UN secretary-general [File: Oliver de Ros/AP Photo]By Stephen QuillenPublished On 16 Nov 202616 Nov 2026
A tense race to replace outgoing United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is heading into its final few weeks in advance of a deadline that has never been breached, as global powers spar over candidates in an opaque election process.
With eight candidates, secret polls and geopolitical rivalries at play, the choice of the UN’s next chief is still up in the air, even as Guterres must leave office on December 31.

Competing interests from the Americas to the Middle East have complicated the process, raising fears that, for the first time in history, the new year could begin without a leader at the helm of the world’s central diplomatic organisation. The late inclusion of two candidates — Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh and Turkish nominee Feridun Sinirlioglu — has further split the race wide open, with no name so far succeeding in overcoming opposition from all five permanent members of the UN Security Council (UNSC), who hold vetoes.
The protracted contest is part of a “struggle over who will exercise political influence within the UN at a time when multilateralism is under considerable pressure and attack”, Georgina Holmes, senior lecturer in politics and international studies at the Open University, United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera.

The widow of Haiti’s slain President Jovenel Moise, whose 2021 ⁠assassination was ⁠a major turning point for the nation, has registered as a candidate for the first presidential election in a decade.
Martine Moise’s name appeared on the website of the Provisional Electoral Council (CEP) as a candidate ⁠on Sunday.

A ⁠first-round vote is set for July next year.
Haiti last held a presidential election in 2016. Successive leaders have repeatedly delayed elections, citing insecurity risks, amid the expanding influence of powerful and heavily armed gangs.
“Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently,” Moise, who has not publicly commented on the registration, said on X last week.
In the post, she also blamed “the opposition” for bringing the country “to its knees”. “They do not want the country to develop; they do not want the people to live well,” she said.
Three female candidates
Martine Moise is one of three ‌women among 33 registered presidential candidates. Among other prominent candidates are Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, both former presidents, former Prime Minister Claude Joseph and former Foreign Minister Dominique Dupuy.

The Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah group has denied its involvement in an oil smuggling operation in Iraq’s Jurf al-Nasr area after Iraqi authorities launched an anticorruption crackdown.

The Iraqi government said an investigation committee, chaired by al-Zaidi, confirmed oil smuggling based on “intelligence documents” containing satellite images showing operations being carried out in the armed faction’s stronghold.

The Singapore-based data centre company said in a statement on Sunday that Alice Huang left her executive role on August 30, 2025, and has held no position with the firm since.

Philippine resupply vessel Unaizah May 4 is hit by a Chinese coastguard's water canon blast in the South China Sea on March 5, 2024 [Aaron Favila/AP]By Al Jazeera Staff, AP and ReutersPublished On 16 Nov 202616 Nov 2026
China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) have failed to conclude long-running negotiations on a code of conduct for the South China Sea during meetings in Manila, despite tentative agreement on about 80 percent of a draft, the Philippines’ foreign minister said.
“There is no conclusion yet,” Theresa Lazaro told reporters at the ASEAN summit on Sunday, adding that several key issues remain unresolved, including whether the code would be legally binding.

ASEAN and Beijing have been working on a code ⁠of conduct in the South China Sea, where they have overlapping claims, for more than two decades. The Philippines, as the current chair of the 11-nation association, had pledged to speed up the process and reach a deal by the end of this year.
Lazaro said she still hoped the code could be concluded under Singapore’s auspices, as the city-state takes over as chair next year.
